sections.heading: When se changes the meaning
sections.body: Many verbs change meaning (or nuance) when used with a reflexive pronoun:

head: Without se
With se
rows: *dormirse* — to fall asleep: *Me dormí en el cine.*
*llevarse* — to take away (with you): *Me llevo este.*
*quedar* — to arrange to meet / be left
*parecerse (a)* — to look like: *Te pareces a tu madre.*
*ponerse* — to put on / become: *Se puso nervioso.*
*comerse* — to eat up (all of it): *Se comió toda la pizza.*
*morirse* — to die (emotional) / be dying to: *Me muero de hambre.*

sections.heading: The "intensifying" se
sections.body: With verbs of consumption (*comer, beber, tomar*) and some others (*saber, leer, ver*), *se* + a specific quantity emphasises completeness: *Me tomé dos cafés.* *Se leyó el libro en un día.* (She read the whole book in a day.) *Me sé la canción de memoria.* (I know the song by heart.)

sections.heading: The dative of interest
sections.body: An indirect pronoun can show who is affected — often emotionally: *No te me pongas triste.* (Don't go getting sad on me.) *Se me murió el perro.* (My dog died — and it affected me.) *Cuídame a los niños.* (Look after the kids for me.) It's very common and colloquial in Latin America.

examples: I fell asleep at the movies.
Me quedo en casa esta noche.
Te pareces mucho a tu madre.
You look a lot like your mother.
Se leyó el libro en un día.
She read the whole book in a day.
Me sé la canción de memoria.
I know the song by heart.
Cuídame a los niños, por favor.
Look after the kids for me, please.
Don't go getting sad on me.
We agreed to meet at eight.
No me acuerdo de su nombre.
